system_prompt:
You are extracting load-bearing passages from one chapter of a guitar method book.

The user will give you the verbatim text of one chapter. Extract every passage
that does any of the following:

- teaches a technique (how to play, fingering, hand position, picking pattern)
- defines a concept (a chord type, a scale, a position system, a terminology)
- gives a rule (when to do X, what to avoid, what to prefer)
- shows a load-bearing example (an exercise that illustrates a method's
  characteristic move)

Output a JSON object with this shape:

  { "quotes": [
      { "topic": "<short topic label>",
        "verbatim_quote": "<exact substring of the input>",
        "why_load_bearing": "<one sentence on why this passage matters>",
        "page": <int, optional>
      },
      ...
  ] }

CRITICAL RULES:
1. `verbatim_quote` MUST be an EXACT substring of the input text. Do not
   paraphrase. Do not add words. Do not fix typos. Copy character-for-character.
2. If you can't find a substantial passage in the input that fits a topic,
   skip the topic — don't fabricate.
3. Skip prose that is purely biographical, motivational, or transitional.
   Keep prose that teaches.
4. Aim for 3-15 quotes per chapter. A chapter with only one load-bearing
   passage gets one quote; a dense chapter gets many.
5. `topic` is a short label (2-6 words). Use the book's own terminology
   when possible.
6. `why_load_bearing` is one sentence in YOUR voice explaining the
   significance — not a paraphrase of the quote.

How to use this book
Although a big part of this method is exclusively dedicated to the guitar, (because it refers to
chord construction and basic visualization of the guitar fretboard),it was created as a tool for all
instruments of all levels (beginner, intermediate and advanced). However, even if you are an
advanced player, make sure you know start at the beginning of the book, otherwise you will
easily get lost by the end of the book.


This method should be used as a dictionary of ideas and techniques. It's important to understand
that the way we approach the musical concepts, ideas and techniques presented here are unique
and cannot be found elsewhere.


Do not worry about learning everything from every chapter. You can go ahead as soon as you
understand the concepts. But always remember that you can come back to any chapter of any
book in order to learn more about a determined subject you want to study again.


Be careful when trying to learn too much at one time. Music is not about quantity but quality.

    Target Tones & Approach Tones
    What is a Target Tone? (also called Target Note)
    We de%ine Target Tones as the main notes of a melody. In other words, the starting notes,
    or ending notes. For example, the “C” major chord can have 3 target tones: C , E and G,
    and any other note we consider as passing notes also called approach notes. However, in
    addition to the chord tones, we can also set the chord tension notes from a determined
    scale as target tones, even if they do not belong to the chord itself.

    It is important to understand that we can only use chord tones or chord tension notes as
    target tones, but not avoid notes. The only exception would be when the avoid note
    becomes part of the chord. Therefore, let’s divide the target tones into two groups:


    a) Chord Target Tones

    b) Scale Target Tones (tension notes)
                                 68



    Types of ApproachTones:
                        46




    After understanding what a Target Tone is, let’s learn about what we call: Approaching
    Tones (passing notes), which are notes that circle the target tones. They are essential to
    get into the jazz improvisational world. We divide them into three different groups:


    1) Scale Tone Approach (Diatonic Approach)

    2 Chromatic Approach (simple, double and triple)

    3) Enclosure Approach

    Scale Tone Approach (Diatonic Approach)
                                                                                                                                          4668




    This type of approaching tone is when you reach the target note by using scale notes
    immediately before or after it. When used over the major scale, it is called Diatonic

    it simply “Scale Tone Approach” (ST). There are four types of ST: simple, double, triple and
    quadruple Scale Tone Approach.
    Notes used immediately before the target tone are called Ascending Scale Tone Approach,
    and notes used immediately after are called Descending Scale Tone Approach. See the

    Chromatic Approach                                                                          4668




    The chromatic approach is one of the oldest and most used concepts in the history of
    western music. This type of approach connects one note to another, using half steps
    between them. We have four chromatic approach possibilities, and each one of them can
    be ascending or descending.

    1) Simple Chromatic

    2) Double Chromatic

    3) Triple Chromatic

    4) Mixed Chromatic

    It is important to understand that depending on the chord, the possibilities of chromatic
    approaches can be different, because the distance from one note to another in each type
    of chord is different.

    Although it is one of the most used approaches in every style of improvisation,
    chromatics must be studied very carefully because the "borderline" between building a
    beautiful melody or a non-musical melody is very thin.
                                68


    1) Simple Chromatic Approach:
                       46




    Simple Chromatic Approach is when you approach a target tone by an ascending half
    step or by a descending half step. It is very important to mention that the simple
    chromatic approach is the only type of chromatic approach that does not require a source
    note to reach the target tone. The simple ascending chromatic approach usually sounds
    more familiar than the simple descending chromatic approach, since every ascending half
    step sounds like a leading one.

3) Mixed Chromatic Approach:
                                                                                                 4668




The Mixed Chromatic Approach is a combination of all types of chromatic approaches with
all types of Scale Tone Approaches, facilitating the melodic chaining between the chords,
and also transforming the common sound of sequential chromatic notes into hybrid
chromatic melodies, which will help us to get free from predictable melodies.

It is important to understand that the Mixed Chromatic Approach needs to have a source
note. In other words, it must start on a chord tone. Notice that in many cases it will contain
only scale notes, which may seem confusing because we could also call this a scale tone
approach.

In order to make this concept clearer we can say that you have to have at least one whole
step combined with one half step before landing on the target tone, independent from
containing only scale tones or mixing scale tones with chromatic notes out of the scale.



Breaking the “Rules”:
The most common way to play chromatics is to play chord tones on the down beats and
chromatic tones on the upbeats. We must be careful to not sound predictable by playing
predetermined rhythmic ideas. Jazz improvisation should sound free Flowing.
                             68


For many years the greatest jazz stars have been teaching us that improvisation is all about
rhythmic and melodic creativity. So why should we be stuck with a preset rhythm every
                    46




time? Remember that in the beginning preset "licks" are very important because we must
learn the "language"of improvisation.

As time goes by and we become more familiar with the "jazz language" we will be releasing
ourselves to play what we hear in our head and in the moment. This is what jazz is about, a
special moment that may not happen again. It is a kind of "musical kaleidoscope" that
shows us something different every time.

In theory, all the mixed chromatic approach possibilities can work ascending or descending.
However, when using double, triple or quadruple chromatics, we must be very careful in
order to not use melodies that might not work. As mentioned before, in many cases the best
option is to use scale tones only.
